entries.title: Job 41:1–8
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: Blood - There are divers eagles who do not feed upon carcases, but many eagles do feed on them. She - In an instant, flying thither with admirable celerity.

entries.title: Job 41:9
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: Hope - The hope of taking or conquering him.

entries.title: Job 41:10
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: Stand - To the battle. Me - To contend with me who created him?

entries.title: Job 41:11
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: Prevented - Hath laid the first obligation upon me, for which I am indebted to him. Who can be before - hand with me in kindnesses, since all things under heaven are mine.

entries.title: Job 41:13
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: Discover - Or, uncover, or take off from him. Face - The upper or outward part of his garment, or, the garment itself: the word face being often redundant. And by the garment is meant the skin which covers the whole body; who dare attempt to touch his very skin? Much less to give him a wound. His double bridle - His fast jaws, which have some resemblance to a double bridle: whence the Greeks call those parts of the face which reach to the jaws on both sides, the bridles.

entries.title: Job 41:14
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: Doors - His mouth. If it be open, none dare enter within, and if it be shut, none dare open it.

entries.title: Job 41:15
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: Shut - Closely compacted together, as things that are fastened together by a seal. This likewise is true of the crocodile, but the skin of the whale is smooth and entire without any scales at all.

entries.title: Job 41:18
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: Sneesings - This the crocodile is said frequently to do. Eyes - To which they seem very fitly compared, because the eyes of the crocodile are dull and dark under the water, but as soon as they appear above water, cast a bright and clear light; like the morning light, suddenly breaking forth after the dark night.

entries.title: Job 41:19
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: Lamps - This also better agrees with the crocodile, which breathes like the river - horse, of which ancient authors affirm, that his nostrils are very large, and he breathes forth a fiery smoke like that of a furnace.

entries.title: Job 41:21
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: Kindleth coals - An hyperbolical expression, denoting extraordinary heat.

entries.title: Job 41:22
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: And sorrow - Sorrow is his companion and harbinger, which attends upon him wheresoever he goes. So anger and fear are said by the poets to accompany the God of war.

entries.title: Job 41:24
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: Nether mill - stone - Which being to bear the weight of the upper, ought to be the harder and stronger of the two.

entries.title: Job 41:25
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: Raiseth - Upon the top of the waters. Mighty - Even the stout - hearted. Breakings - By reason of their great danger and distress; which is expressed by this very word, Psal 60:2 Jonah 2:4. Purify - Those who ordinarily live in the neglect of God, they cry unto God in their trouble, and endeavour to purge their consciences from the guilt of their sins.

entries.title: Job 41:26
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: Hold - Heb. cannot stand, cannot endure the stroke, but will be broken by it. The crocodile's skin, no sword, nor dart, nor musquet bullet can pierce.

entries.title: Job 41:28
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: Turned - Hurt him no more than a blow with a little stubble.

entries.title: Job 41:30
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: Stones - His skin is so impenetrable, that the sharpest stones or shells are as easy unto him as the mire.

entries.title: Job 41:31
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: Boil - To swell, and foam, and froth by his strong and vehement motion, as any liquor does when it is boiled in a pot, especially boiling ointment. The sea - The great river Nile, is called a sea, both in scripture, as Isa 11:15, and in other authors, as Euphrates is called the sea of Babylon, Isa 21:1 Jer 51:36. Lakes also are most frequently called seas both in the Old and New Testament: and in such lakes the crocodiles are as well as in the Nile.

entries.title: Job 41:32
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: Shine - By the white froth or foam upon the waters. The same may be observed in the wake of a ship by night.

entries.title: Job 41:34–42:1
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: King, &c. - He can tame both the behemoth and leviathan, as strong and stout - hearted as they are. This discourse concerning them was brought in, to prove that it is God only, who can look upon proud men and abase them, bring them low, and hide them in the dust, he it is that beholdeth all high things, and wherein men dealt proudly, he is above them. He is king over all the children of pride, brutal or rational, and makes them either bend or break before him.
